An obituary is a written announcement that a person has died, published in a newspaper, magazine, or website. But it is much more than just a death announcement — it is a short biography of the person's life, written at the time of their death, so that the world can remember who they were.

Think of it this way: when someone dies, an obituary answers two questions at once — "When did they die?" and "Who were they when they were alive?"

A typical obituary includes:

  • The person's full name and sometimes a nickname they were known by
  • Their age and the date they died
  • A brief life story — where they were born, where they grew up, what they did for work, what they were passionate about
  • Their achievements — things they accomplished in life, awards, contributions to their community
  • Their family members — who they are survived by (spouse, children, siblings, grandchildren) and sometimes who died before them
  • Funeral or memorial service details — when and where people can come to pay their respects
  • Sometimes, the cause of death, though this is not always included
Who Writes It and Where It Appears

Obituaries are most commonly written by:

  • Journalists at newspapers, who write them for well-known or notable people
  • Family members, who write them for their loved ones and submit them to a local newspaper or funeral home website
  • Funeral homes, which often help families draft one

You will find obituaries in:

  • The pages of local and national newspapers (there is often a dedicated "Obituaries" section)
  • Online news websites
  • Funeral home websites
  • Community notice boards

An obituary serves several important purposes:

  1. It informs the community that someone has passed away, so friends, colleagues, and acquaintances who may not have heard the news can find out.
  2. It honors the person's life by highlighting their journey, personality, and legacy.
  3. It preserves their memory — obituaries are often saved by families as a permanent record, almost like a historical document of a person's existence.
  4. It invites people to mourn together by sharing the details of the funeral or memorial service.

Obituaries are written in a respectful, dignified, and warm tone. They focus on celebrating the person's life rather than dwelling on the sadness of their death. Even if the person had a difficult life, an obituary generally highlights the good — their kindness, their humor, their love for their family, their hard work.

Since you want a complete picture, it helps to know how an obituary differs from things that seem similar:

  • Death notice vs. obituary: A death notice is very short — just a sentence or two simply announcing that someone has died, often placed as a classified ad. An obituary is longer and tells the story of the person's life. Think of a death notice as a telegram and an obituary as a letter.
  • Eulogy vs. obituary: A eulogy is a speech delivered out loud at a funeral or memorial service, usually by a close friend or family member. An obituary is written and published for the general public. Both honor the deceased, but a eulogy is spoken and private (to those at the funeral), while an obituary is written and public.
  • Biography vs. obituary: A biography is a full, in-depth account of someone's life, often book-length. An obituary is a short, condensed version — essentially a mini-biography written specifically because the person has just died.

Here are examples to show you how the word is naturally used:

  • "I read her obituary in the newspaper this morning."
  • "His family asked the funeral home to help them write an obituary."
  • "The obituary described him as a devoted father and talented musician."
  • "She worked for years as an obituary writer at a local newspaper."
  • "The obituaries section is usually near the back of the newspaper."

The plural of obituary is simply obituaries.

  • "The newspaper published three obituaries on Tuesday."
  • "She flipped to the obituaries page every morning."

Obituaries are not only written for ordinary people — they are also written for famous individuals like presidents, scientists, artists, and athletes. When a very famous person dies, major newspapers like The New York Times or The Guardian publish long, detailed obituaries that can run for several pages. In fact, large newspapers keep pre-written obituaries ready for very old or ill celebrities, so they can publish them immediately when the person passes away. This is a normal journalistic practice and not considered disrespectful.

Also, the word obituary can occasionally be used figuratively — for example, someone might say "That was the obituary of our friendship," meaning the moment their friendship permanently ended. This usage is literary and not common in everyday speech, but you may encounter it in books or articles.

If you had to explain "obituary" to someone in a single sentence:

An obituary is a written tribute published when someone dies, combining the announcement of their death with a brief, respectful account of their life, so the world can know who they were and how to say goodbye.
